strengths: High-quality asset creation: ArtVIP provides 992 professionally crafted articulated assets across 37 subcategories in the modern USD format, addressing a critical bottleneck in visual realism and physics fidelity present in older datasets like PartNet-Mobility and BEHAVIOR-1K.

Well-formulated physical and modular interaction primitives: The paper formalizes five canonical interaction behaviors (e.g., magnetic latching, damping, position-triggered thresholds, within-asset linkage) directly embedded into the joint dynamics formulations, reducing scripting overhead in simulators like Isaac Sim.

Comprehensive empirical verification: The authors validate asset realism quantitatively across multiple dimensions, including visual geometry (triangle counts and reconstruction via VGGT), visual semantics (CLIP feature distributions), and physical dynamics (optical motion capture tracking under calibrated forces).

Rigorous real-world robotic evaluation: Extensive real-robot manipulation experiments on Franka Emika Panda arms across multiple tasks (PullDrawer, OpenCabinet, SlideShelf, CloseOven) using both Action Chunking Transformer (ACT) and Diffusion Policy (DP), demonstrating zero-shot sim-to-real transfer and clear advantages over PartNet-Mobility.
weaknesses: Scalability bottleneck: The asset creation relies entirely on manual labor by professional 3D artists and manual parameter tuning (thousands of hours reported in Table 4), making dataset expansion difficult to scale compared to procedural or automated generative methods.

Evaluation scope on downstream tasks: Although the dataset covers 37 diverse subcategories (such as tools, stationery, and small appliances), the real-world manipulation experiments are largely confined to standard cabinet/drawer/microwave pulling and closing tasks, leaving more intricate articulated objects untested.

Limited algorithmic novelty: The contribution is predominantly centered on asset engineering, dataset compilation, and simulator parameterization; the robotic learning algorithms used (ACT, DP, EAGLE, PPO) are standard off-the-shelf methods.

Missing release link: The abstract leaves the open-source repository link empty ('Our data are available at:'), making it harder to verify the immediate usability and structure of the released USD files during review.

strengths: High-quality asset suite: ArtVIP provides 992 expertly modeled, high-fidelity articulated digital twins across 37 subcategories, accompanied by 6 fully interactable sim-ready indoor scenes and pixel-level affordance annotations in native USD format.

Sophisticated physical and interactive modeling: The paper explicitly tackles complex real-world articulation dynamics often neglected in simulation (e.g., latch release, non-linear damping, door closer mechanics, position-dependent joint stiffness), and quantitatively verifies these dynamics using an optical motion tracking system against real-world counterparts.

Comprehensive downstream robotics evaluations: The utility and fidelity of the assets are validated through extensive real-world robot manipulation experiments using both imitation learning (ACT, Diffusion Policy across 4 tasks) and reinforcement learning (EAGLE PPO on Franka), showing strong sim-to-real transfer and clear improvements over prior datasets like PartNet-Mobility.

Solid technical analysis and comparisons: The paper thoroughly profiles the trade-offs between visual/geometric fidelity and simulation frame rates, compares CLIP feature distributions with real imagery, and benchmarks against recent generative 3D articulation methods (e.g., SplArt).
weaknesses: Scalability bottleneck: As acknowledged by the authors, the asset creation and physics parameter tuning pipeline relies heavily on professional 3D modelers and manual tuning (averaging several hours per object), which constrains rapid scaling compared to automated reconstruction or generative approaches.

Breadth of real-world RL validation: While the imitation learning experiments span four diverse tasks and comparative digital-cousin evaluations, the real-world RL evaluation is demonstrated on a single task (CloseTrashcan).

Engine-specific joint parameterization: The extended joint drive formulations are implemented specifically within Isaac Sim/PhysX; although export tools to URDF/MJCF are mentioned, reproducing state-dependent joint behaviors (such as non-linear stiffness curves and latch release triggers) in other physics engines (e.g., MuJoCo, Bullet) may require custom plugin logic.

strengths: High practical significance and impact: High-quality, physically accurate articulated assets are a major bottleneck in embodied AI and robotic manipulation. ArtVIP delivers 992 carefully authored articulated assets across 37 subcategories and 6 fully interactive scenes in modern USD format.

Rigorous physical and kinematic modeling: Beyond visual realism, the authors put substantial effort into modeling realistic joint dynamics (such as position-dependent stiffness, latching mechanisms, and velocity-dependent friction), validated quantitatively against real-world optical motion capture tracking data.

Embedded modular interaction primitives: Abstracting and embedding canonical interaction behaviors (e.g., magnetic closure, damping, cross-asset triggers) directly within the assets greatly facilitates simulation workflow and asset reusability without requiring bespoke simulation scripting.

Extensive real-robot downstream validation: The paper validates the utility of the assets across both imitation learning (ACT, Diffusion Policy across four manipulation tasks) and reinforcement learning (EAGLE sim-to-real on Franka arm), including direct digital-cousin comparisons against PartNet-Mobility.
weaknesses: High manual modeling overhead and scalability constraints: As reported in Table 4, each asset requires several hours of professional 3D modeling and tuning, which poses a significant hurdle for scaling up the dataset compared to procedural or generative pipelines.

Limited variety of real-world evaluation instances: While the physical hardware experiments are impressive, the sim-to-real transfer experiments are tested on a small set of physical object instances (e.g., a single unseen microwave model for the comparative imitation learning experiment), leaving open how robustly these findings generalize across wider within-category variations in the physical world.

Minor inconsistencies and formalization details: In Section 3.2 and Appendix E, the friction formulation (Eq. 3a–3c) mixes notation (|F| + |T| with dimensional mismatch between force and torque) without explicitly stating the normalization or contact point radii. In addition, the text in Section 5.3 mentions evaluation across checkpoints from 300k–500k iterations, whereas Table 3 lists checkpoints starting from 100k.
